title: Fine-tuning and Post-training
premise: Where a base model becomes a product, and where the evaluation discipline from AIE-102 stops being optional. The single question this course exists to answer honestly is the one most fine-tuning write-ups avoid: did it beat a well-prompted baseline on the same eval set? Frequently it does not, and a course that cannot produce that answer has taught a technique rather than a judgement.
why_here: Twelfth overall, after transformers because a fine-tune you cannot picture as a change to specific weights is a black box with a price tag, and after evaluation because the entire value here is a comparison. It is the first course with two prerequisites, and both are load-bearing.
laboratory: Career Side Quests' evidence extraction, because the eval already exists. You built a 30-case gold set for it in AIE-102 and the harness that runs it in tools/eval-harness — which means the measurement predates the model. That is the correct order and almost never how it happens in practice, and having it means every claim in this course is checkable rather than asserted.
compute_note: Everything here runs on a small open model of a few hundred million parameters, with LoRA, on free-tier hosted compute or CPU where it fits. Paid API fine-tuning is explicitly not required: it hides the mechanism behind a service, and a course that costs money to attempt is a course that gets skipped. Where an item needs more compute than that, it says so and offers a smaller substitute.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. The portfolio contains no fine-tune, no curated training set and no preference data, and prompt engineering at scale is not evidence about weight updates.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Judges are instructed that a submission concluding the fine-tune did not beat the prompted baseline is not thereby weaker. The criterion throughout is the quality of the comparison, not whether the fashionable technique won.

items.title: The post-training pipeline, end to end
Training language models to follow instructions
Inclusion rules, written before the data
checkpoints: Inclusion and exclusion rules written before any example is collected
At least 100 candidate examples assembled
Every example accepted or rejected against the written rules
Rejections counted by rule, and the rules revised once with the revision logged
items.brief: Write the inclusion and exclusion rules for a fine-tuning dataset before you look at any candidate data, then collect at least a hundred candidates and judge every one against the rules. Count the rejections by rule. You will find at least one rule that rejects nothing, which means it was decoration, and at least one that turns out to be ambiguous in practice. Revise once and log what changed. The dataset is the model, and rules invented while filtering are rules fitted to the data you happened to have.

items.title: How ambiguous are your own rules
checkpoints: A sample re-judged after a gap of at least a day
Self-agreement measured on identical items
Disagreements traced to specific rules
Rules rewritten where the disagreement was linguistic rather than substantive
items.brief: Take fifty examples you already judged, wait at least a day, and judge them again without looking at your earlier answers. Measure how often you agree with yourself. Anything below near-total agreement is a measurement of how ambiguous your rules are, not of your concentration — and it puts a ceiling on what any model trained on this data can learn. Trace each disagreement to a rule and rewrite the rules that caused them.

items.title: Llama 2, for the post-training section
Run a supervised fine-tune
checkpoints: A small open model chosen and its size stated
Loss masked so only completion tokens contribute
Training and validation loss recorded
Evaluated on the AIE-102 gold set through the harness
items.brief: Fine-tune a small open model on the dataset you curated. Mask the loss so that only the completion tokens contribute — verify this by checking that the prompt tokens' gradients are zero, because getting it wrong produces a model that trains without error and learns to predict its own prompts. Evaluate through the harness on the gold set that already existed, not on a metric invented afterwards.

items.title: The prompted baseline that has to lose first
checkpoints: A genuine prompt-engineering effort on the base model, time-boxed and logged
Few-shot examples drawn from the same training data
Evaluated on the identical gold set
The comparison stated with an interval, not a point
items.brief: Spend real effort prompting the base model to do the same task — few-shot examples drawn from the same data your fine-tune saw, a time-box you state in advance, and the iterations logged. Evaluate on the identical gold set through the same harness. Then state the comparison with an interval rather than two bare numbers. If the prompted baseline wins, that is the finding, and it is the most commercially useful sentence in this course.

items.title: Rank is a dial with a cost
checkpoints: Three ranks trained on identical data and schedule
Trainable parameter count reported per rank
Gold-set score reported per rank
Training time and memory recorded per rank
items.brief: Train the same fine-tune at three LoRA ranks. Report trainable parameters, gold-set score, wall-clock and peak memory for each. Plot score against trainable parameters. The interesting region is where the curve flattens, because that is the rank above which you are paying for nothing — and it is usually lower than the defaults suggest.

items.title: Where the low-rank assumption runs out
checkpoints: A task chosen where LoRA is expected to struggle, with the reason stated first
LoRA and full fine-tuning both run where compute allows
The gap measured, or the substitute experiment justified
The low-rank assumption stated in terms of what it constrains
items.brief: LoRA constrains the update to a low-rank subspace, which is an assumption about how much the weights need to move. Construct or choose a task where you expect that assumption to bind — a large domain shift rather than a format change — and predict the outcome before running it. Compare against full fine-tuning if compute allows; if it does not, say so and substitute a smaller model where it does. State the assumption in mechanical terms: what kind of change can a rank-r update not express.

items.title: The DPO loss, from the equation
checkpoints: The loss implemented directly from the paper's equation
Reference-model log-probabilities handled explicitly
Verified against the library implementation on identical inputs
The role of beta demonstrated at two values
items.brief: Implement the DPO loss from the equation in the paper, not from the library. Handle the reference model explicitly — the frozen policy's log-probabilities are where implementations diverge quietly. Verify against the library on identical inputs and weights. Then show what beta does by running two values and describing the behaviour, since it controls how far the policy is allowed to move and is the parameter people set by copying.

items.title: Run DPO, and find what else moved
checkpoints: A small preference set built with the preference criterion stated
DPO run from an SFT checkpoint
The targeted behaviour measured before and after
At least two untargeted capabilities measured before and after
items.brief: Build a small preference dataset — pairs where you can state why one response is preferred — and run DPO from your SFT checkpoint. Measure the behaviour you targeted. Then measure at least two things you did not target and did not want to change. Preference optimisation moves the whole policy, and the untargeted measurements are the point of the assignment.

items.title: Regression sweep on what you did not intend to change
checkpoints: A capability set defined before fine-tuning, covering behaviours not being targeted
Base model scored on all of them
Fine-tuned model scored on the identical set
Regressions reported individually rather than as an average
items.brief: Define a set of capabilities you are not trying to change — instruction following on unrelated tasks, formatting, refusal behaviour, another language — and score the base model on all of them before fine-tuning. Score the fine-tuned model on the identical set afterwards. Report each individually. Averaging hides exactly the failure this exists to find, which is a large regression in one capability concealed by small gains in several.

items.title: fine-tune-study, published
checkpoints: Public write-up with the dataset rules, the training configuration and the eval
The prompted baseline comparison stated prominently rather than buried
A negative result included
Connected backwards to the AIE-102 gold set and the harness
items.brief: Publish the study that the fine-tuning capability claim points at: the curation rules, what the data looked like, the training configuration, and the comparison against a well-prompted baseline on a gold set that predated the model. The comparison goes near the top, not in a discussion section at the end. It must connect backwards to AIE-102's gold set and to the harness that ran it, because the fact that the measurement existed first is the strongest thing about this piece of work.

items.title: The alignment tax, measured on your own model
checkpoints: A refusal or safety behaviour identified in the base model
Measured before and after both SFT and DPO stages
Any change reported including a loosening
The mechanism suggested rather than asserted
items.brief: Pick a safety behaviour the base model exhibits and measure it before your SFT, after your SFT, and after DPO. Fine-tuning on narrow task data routinely erodes behaviours nobody intended to touch, and reporting a loosening in your own model is the honest outcome here. Suggest a mechanism for what you observe, and mark it as a suggestion rather than a finding.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes. This defense carries the fine-tuning capability claim.
sample_question_shapes: Your self-agreement on the labels was below ceiling. What does that put a limit on, and how would you have raised it?
You chose rank 16. Talk me through what a rank-4 update cannot express that a rank-16 one can, without using the word 'capacity'.
Your prompted baseline beat the fine-tune. A stakeholder has already told the client you are fine-tuning. What do you say to them?

rubrics.integrity: This defense carries the fine-tuning capability claim. A candidate who concedes that the prompted baseline won, and can say precisely why, scores higher than one who defends the fine-tune past the evidence.

completion.required: All nine assignments, the project and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on all four fine-tuning skills and contributes to alignment techniques, making the Fine-tuning and post-training capability claimable. FSRS then decays them.
